What I did

I updated Jaime’s regressions for phase 2b. Each AI model has one binomial logistic regression fitted to votes with a winner. A question can have several features at once. The model estimates the chance of a win on a decisive vote given those features.

The descriptive fit below uses 77,843 decisive votes from April through July, represented by two model-side rows per vote. There are 48 fitted models. As in Jaime’s original code, flagged review cases are excluded from the fit. The original data are unchanged.

Response and predictors

The response is 1 for a win and 0 for a loss. These are the only predictors; all describe the question, before the AI writes an answer.

Feature Meaning
is_code The question involves programming.
math The question involves mathematics.
creative_writing The question asks for creative writing.
instruction_following The question contains specific instructions.
complexity The question is complex.
creativity The task needs creative thinking.
domain_knowledge The task needs subject knowledge.
problem_solving The task needs problem-solving steps.
real_world The task has a practical, real-world use.
specificity The task is specific and well defined.
technical_accuracy The task needs technical accuracy.

Response length, formatting, price and tokens are not predictors. The opponent is not a predictor in these separate regressions (group decision 5).

This is the actual regression specification:

glm(y ~ is_code + math + creative_writing + instruction_following +
      complexity + creativity + domain_knowledge + problem_solving +
      real_world + specificity + technical_accuracy,
    family = binomial(), data = votes_for_one_model)

The main fit uses standard logistic regression. The half-point quasibinomial fit remains available as a sensitivity check. Ridge is optional and the descriptive results below use no penalty.

The regressions: full R output

A positive math coefficient means a higher fitted win probability on math questions, holding the other features fixed. It is a change in log-odds, not a percentage-point change or a causal effect. For example, Gemini’s math coefficient is 0.205. P-values below are nominal: the rows are not independent across models.

Open each example to see its complete summary() output, including coefficients, deviance and convergence information. The third example has the fewest votes in this descriptive fit.

Feature effects for all 48 models

Blue means a higher fitted win probability when a feature is present; red means a lower probability. These are log-odds coefficients, with the other features held fixed. The intercept is omitted from this chart. Full values, including all intercepts, are in R/resultados/coeficientes_por_modelo.csv.

Descriptive fit with decisive April–July votes and no ridge.

Does it predict unseen votes?

The descriptive fit above uses all months. The test below uses a separate fit. The table below comes directly from Mark’s saved evaluation. Mark fits on April–June only and evaluates decisive July votes where both models were seen in train. All three methods in this table use decisive votes for training.

Method July votes Correct Accuracy (%) Log-loss (lower is better)
General Bradley–Terry ranking 20416 13164 64.5 0.6340
General win rate 20416 13162 64.5 0.6340
Separate binomial regressions 20416 13303 65.2 0.6298

The separate regressions gain 0.68 percentage points in accuracy over the general Bradley–Terry ranking. They also have lower log-loss on this July test.

Sensitivity check

With the optional quasibinomial fit, ties and votes where both answers were bad each receive half a point in training. On the same decisive July votes, this version achieved 65.1% accuracy and 0.6321 log-loss.

Top 3 by task

top3() averages fitted win probabilities over real questions with each feature, allowing the other features to vary. The descriptive fit uses decisive votes from all four months. Only models with at least 100 votes in July can be recommended. Versions remain separate. These scores rank the models for each task. Each model has its own fitted probability.

An optional budget filters output price per million tokens, not total cost per answer. Unknown prices are excluded only when a budget is supplied. The budget example uses Marco’s v2 price table, as required by this task. List prices do not measure the full cost of a reasoning response. For example:

top3("math", ajustes, precio_max = 2)

Limits and next step

  • Each vote contributes two model-side rows; the separate fits are dependent.
  • The main test is one time split, April–June versus July.
  • Four models appear only in July and cannot be tested with that training set.

The combined Bradley–Terry model is a separate next task. It will use one row per vote and account directly for the opponent. This report does not include it.

Prepared by Nessim Betesh with assistance from ChatGPT/Codex. Existing model code by Jaime and held-out evaluation by Mark. AI-generated code and text were checked against the repository’s data, saved outputs and rules.
